shared/clippings/deep-work.title: MIT PhD taught me to unlock my brain’s “Sage Mode” - Deep Work (Full Summary)
shared/clippings/deep-work.content:
Interesting video, it just lacks the aspect of being truly interested in your field to be more easily entering deep work.

Detailed summary of Deep Work by Cal Newport.
The most important skill you can learn this decade is how to 100x your brain power so that you can easily reach the top 10% of your industry in terms of skill and pay.
This lets you get rich faster so you can spend your evenings and weekends doing fun stuff and adventuring.
*** TIMESTAMPS ***
0:00 Intro
1:26 Why You Need To Learn Deep Work
3:07 Method 1
3:56 Method 2
5:39 Method 3
6:37 Method 4
7:16 Method 5
8:28 Method 6
10:10 Method 7
10:53 Method 8
11:48 Method 9
12:22 Method 10
Thank you for watching! Please like and subscribe to support the channel :)
Transcript
Intro
0:00 · There’s one skill that can make you more money than crypto, stocks, and real estate combined. And that skill ising, but that’s illegal. So, the next best skill you can learn is how to master the art of deep work. You see, right now, there’s a lot of really smart people in the world, and they’re all trying to collect money. You’re also trying to collect money, but they’re smarter than you. So, you’re basically trying to compete in a Fortnite tournament while running Windows 95.
0:22 · If you learn how to train your brain to easily enter a deep work state, it’ll basically be like going back in time to before they had calculators while you have a phone running the latest version of DeepSeek.
0:35 · So, how can you learn how to do this?
0:36 · It’s actually really easy. There’s a guy named Cal Newport who wrote a book called Deep Work, which I’m going to summarize for you here. But why should you listen to him instead of your favorite productivity blogger with a ring light? It’s because Cal is a theoretical computer scientist from MIT.
0:50 · And in his book, he teaches the same techniques that he himself used to earn a topranked PhD, publish four books, and double his rate of writing peer-reviewed academic papers while never working past 5:00 p.m. Also, because science, there was a study that interviewed 50 ultra highscoring college students from the most competitive schools, and they found that the top ranking students actually spent less time studying than the group of students right below them in the rankings.
1:16 · They did this because they learned how to maximize their brain’s ability to focus at super saiyan levels at will, while you were learning how to analyze charts to day trade Dogecoin.
Why You Need To Learn Deep Work
1:27 · I’m going to teach you all the skills from the book on how to activate your brain’s sage mode in just a minute. But first, you must listen to my tale.
1:34 · Please give me 47 seconds to convince you why not watching this video in full would be a worse decision for your life than taking advice on where to invest your life savings from sports players and Larry David. One, the world has become way more globalized. 50 years ago, if you were a mediocre programmer living in Boise, Idaho, you could pretty easily get a cushy tech job at your local Standard Potato and provide for your second wife and three stepchildren.
1:59 · But today, Standard Potato doesn’t have to settle for the talent pool of Idaho.
2:03 · They can recruit and hire people from anywhere. Like the far superior talent pool in Ohio or Sergey from Estonia who’s willing to work for onetenth your salary cuz $500 will buy enough smoked sprouts and Estonian cheese to feed his family for a lifetime. What this means is that low to mid-level knowledge work is becoming commoditized. The only way you can compete for the big bucks is by becoming extremely skilled, like the top 10% in a particular specialty. Don’t worry, this is actually really easy.
2:32 · Two, working on anything while not in a deep work state eats away at your free time. Because if your entire life is just spending 12 hours a day on working or studying, cuz that’s the only way you can earn enough money to feed your second wife and three stepchildren, then that’s not a very fun way to live. The goal is to get your brain so supercharged that you can knock out more highquality work in 2 hours than you typically do in 8, leaving the rest of the day wide open for you to binge watch a show you’ll forget existed by next Tuesday.
2:58 · Anyways, here’s 11 ways the book teaches you to unlock your brain’s ability to 10x both its speed and the quality of work it produces. One, be very selective about your work environment. Before JK Rowling waged war on trans people, she actually wrote a pretty famous book called Harry Potter.
Method 1
3:17 · Trying to write the book at home was really distracting because of the kids running around, the dogs barking, the cleaners working, and the activists protesting outside her window. So, she changed up her scenery by checking into a suite at the five-star Balmoral Hotel in downtown Edinburgh, which is one of the most luxurious Victorian stone buildings in the city. And it’s right across the street from Edinburghough Castle, which was one of Rowling’s inspirations for Hogwarts. This was really effective cuz not only were there no distractions, but the vibes were also perfect for creative writing.
3:44 · And since she paid more money to spend time there than the yearly salary of a public school teacher, it forced her brain to buckle down and focus with 100% efficiency to avoid feeling like she’s wasting money. Two, your time boxes have to be made of cast iron. It actually doesn’t matter if you spend time doom scrolling or keeping up with the Kardashians. Cal Newport says you don’t need to bother with avoiding or even reducing how much time you spend on distracting behavior.
Method 2
4:10 · The only thing that matters is that when you do schedule your actual deep work time blocks where you promise yourself that you’re going to focus on something really important, you make sure that you don’t get distracted no matter what during those time blocks. You can start with short time blocks like 30 minutes and eventually work your way up to a few hours. Here’s why this is so important.
4:32 · Imagine that when you scheduled your time blocks for the day, you put up a physical wall between your deep focus time and your shallow activities time.
4:40 · Every single time you let your brain convince you to cross that wall, even for small stuff like checking your Instagram for 2 seconds, what’s actually happening is you’re drilling a physical hole through that wall so that you can pass through. And the more often you do this, the more holes you’re drilling through that wall until there are so many holes that your brain is just going to ignore that wall altogether. Which means that the next time you want to put up that mental focus wall to concentrate on something really important, you won’t be able to keep your thoughts focused on the task at hand.
5:08 · Your thoughts are just going to keep hopping back and forth between studying for your final exam for 5 minutes and thinking about whether a 100 men can defeat a silverback gorilla in unarmed combat for 3 and 1/2 hours.
5:20 · Cuz your mental wall that’s supposed to keep your concentration boxed in is going to have more holes than Jeffrey Epstein’s prison security footage. But the more times you fight against that urge for distraction during your scheduled deep work time, the more your brain patches up these holes, making it really easy to stay in an ultra focus mode whenever you schedule it. Three, don’t plan your day like a fool. Studies show that when it comes to estimating how much time a certain activity will take, humans are more delusional than an unemployed influencer calling himself a disruptor after using chat GBT to vibe code a worse version of Craigslist.
Method 3
5:54 · People who estimated they watch an average of 15 hours of TV each week actually watch closer to 30 when the data was tracked. And when it comes to work, it was the opposite. People estimate they spend twice as much time working as they actually do in reality.
6:08 · To fix this, do these three things.
6:11 · Single eye, schedule your day in batches of similar tasks cuz your brain wastes a lot of energy whenever it switches from one type of task to a different one. Two eyes, schedule your deep work as early in the day as possible because that’s when you have the most brain energy.
6:26 · Three eyes, schedule buffer and contingency to allow for flexibility cuz you’re probably going to miscalculate how long stuff will take you and you don’t want those miscalculations to throw off your plan. But you probably aren’t taking notes and it’s hard to remember all these things. So method four is to create a ritual that you do right before you enter deep work. This will make entering a deep work state eventually become easy and automatic after you do your ritual.
Method 4
6:50 · This could be something as simple like making coffee and putting on jazz music or something more complicated like drawing a pentagram and espresso grounds and summoning your productivity demon. If you do this every day for a few weeks, your brain will just automatically enter an ultra focused deep work state as soon as you draw the pentagram because you’ve built that habit loop. Just like you automatically reach for a towel after washing your hands without spending any energy thinking about it. Method five is to use idle gaps like a smart person.
Method 5
7:20 · Entering deep work isn’t a one-time decision. It’s not something you try once like tofu or krypto. It’s a real muscle that will atrophy if you don’t exercise it. But people treat focus like it’s a personality trait. Oh, I just can’t concentrate. I must be neurode divergent. But it’s all about how you train your brain.
7:37 · Cuz people who constantly try to fill up any moments of boredom with some type of distraction, like scrolling TikTok when you’re at the dentist office before they glue your teeth back together, have immeasurably different brain wiring than people who train themselves to be comfortable with sitting in silence. If every day you practice being able to just sit there without any external stimulation, like when you’re in line at the grocery store or waiting for your water to boil, this will make it way easier to comfortably sit in silence and boredom when working on difficult problems.
8:06 · If you can’t handle even a few minutes of bored silence, your brain will definitely not be able to handle getting stuck on hard problems and will immediately trigger you to start doomcrolling at the first sign of mild stress. Cal Newport once said, “Once you’re wired for distraction, you crave it.” Then he went to go silently stare at a tree for 45 minutes. Method six is to multitask the right way instead of the wrong way. The way most people multitask is wrong.
Method 6
8:32 · What they try to do is flip back and forth between two cognitive tasks, like checking emails and working on a project. Studies have shown that this literally turns your brain into mashed potatoes with Wi-Fi. That’s not even a joke. The book suggests that you take advantage of tasks you already do that require no mental brain power, like walking your dog or commuting to work, and use that time to think deeply about a creative problem you need to solve.
9:00 · So, the next time you’re out walking on your lunch break from work, instead of chain smoking cigarettes, try thinking about how to name your Etsy shop side hustle without sounding like a cult. If your boss asks, “What took you so long?”
9:12 · You can tell them that you were implementing mobile strategic ideiation.
9:16 · The whole point is to give your brain practice with picking one important topic and working through that one topic from start to finish without getting distracted. This will turn your mind into the brain equivalent of Arnold Schwarzenegger. And by multitasking this with an activity you already do that requires zero brain power. You don’t need to find any extra time in your day to do this brain training. Something to keep in mind is that when you first try this, your brain’s going to fill up with a bunch of less important, more entertaining thoughts like, “Do raccoons have knees?” or “Could essential oils cure your uncle’s dyslexia?”
9:48 · If these come to mind, just remind yourself that you can worry about that later and come back to thinking about your main task at hand. You should also structure your thinking process so that you’re tackling key questions one at a time and then summarizing your conclusions at the end of your thinking session instead of just randomly bouncing around different topics over and over again. Method seven is you should become irresponsible not by microwaving foil but by taking on less responsibilities.
Method 7
10:15 · This will give you more time and energy to get smart or to follow your dreams of becoming a professional ice cream taster. Physicist Richard Fineman was a self-proclaimed irresponsible person. Whenever someone asked him to take on more responsibilities like being on fancy committees or doing admin work, he just said, “Nah, I’m good.” Then he won a Nobel Prize cuz he had time to focus on the important stuff. Cal Newport says, “Clarity about what matters provides clarity about what does not.”
10:42 · And this quote helped me a lot cuz once I understood that life is meaningless and the universe is silent, I stopped worrying about optimizing my notion dashboard. Method eight is to avoid the any benefit mind trap. Your brain likes to do low value shallow tasks because they require less brain energy, but it knows you don’t want to do low value tasks. So, it tries to trick you by rationalizing the value that you do get from them. Like scrolling Facebook lets you keep up with what’s going on in the lives of people you knew from high school.
Method 8
11:12 · But let’s be honest, if you didn’t read that Sharon from 2009 is feeling blessed at a cheesecake factory, I promise you’d still wake up tomorrow with the same credit score and slightly crooked spine. Meanwhile, that time and energy could have gone to literally anything better, like learning a skill that makes you rich, growing your own strawberries, or making actual real friends in real life. Just because an option has some benefit, doesn’t mean it’s a good choice.
11:37 · Newport says you should identify the highest ROI tasks and use your deep work time blocks to focus exclusively on those because that’s how you make your life actually better. Method 9 is to end your day the right way and not the wrong way. Trying to squeeze out a little extra work at night is actually bad. What’s better is to let your brain fully relax for the evening, but your brain can’t fully relax if it’s stressing out about unresolved tasks.
Method 9
12:02 · So, what you should do is spend the last 15 minutes of your workday listing out all the urgent and important items left on your to-do list and writing down a plan for how you plan to tackle each of them tomorrow. That way, your brain can actually relax and recharge cuz it knows that you already have a written plan in place and that there’s nothing to worry about. # Documentation: the four-quadrant system

Based on the Divio documentation system (Daniele Procida, docs.divio.com/documentation-system/).

There is no single thing called "documentation". There are four kinds, and they
serve different readers with different needs. Each needs its own document.

## The two axes

|                 | Study (learning)         | Work (doing)                |
| --------------- | ------------------------ | --------------------------- |
| **Practical**   | Tutorial                 | How-to guide                |
| **Theoretical** | Explanation              | Reference                   |

## The cardinal rule

**Never mix quadrants inside one document.** Almost every documentation failure
is a quadrant violation:

- explanation smuggled into a tutorial ("before we continue, note that Django's
  ORM uses the active-record pattern...") — the beginner stalls
- how-to steps buried in reference — the fact becomes unfindable
- reference tables inside a tutorial — the learner loses the thread
- a tutorial that stops to offer three alternative approaches — the learner now
  has to make a decision they lack the knowledge to make

When a section starts serving a second quadrant, cut it out and link to it.

---

## 1. Tutorial — learning-oriented

**Analogy:** teaching a child to cook. The dish barely matters; the confidence
and the craft knowledge do.

**Purpose:** take a beginner by the hand through a series of steps to complete a
meaningful project, so they finish knowing they *can*.

MUST:
- work reliably, every time, on every supported system — a broken tutorial
  destroys trust faster than no tutorial
- produce a visible, comprehensible result at every step
- build progressively: simplest concrete action first
- take full responsibility for the journey; the author decides what is learned
- keep explanation to the bare minimum needed to proceed

MUST NOT:
- ask the learner to appreciate an abstraction before they have met the concrete
- include extended discussion (important — just not here)
- mention alternatives, options, or "you could also..."
- show advanced technique or best practice

**Test:** a motivated beginner following it word for word ends with a working
thing and no unresolved confusion.

---

## 2. How-to guide — goal-oriented

**Analogy:** a recipe. Assumes you can already cook.

**Purpose:** answer a specific question that only a user with some competence can
even pose. "How do I ...?"

MUST:
- be titled `How to <do the thing>` — "How to create a web form", never a noun
  phrase like "Class-based views"
- give steps in a working sequence
- stay practical: **usability beats completeness**
- allow flexibility so the reader can adapt it to their near-miss situation
- link out for concepts rather than explaining them inline

MUST NOT:
- teach the basics the reader already has
- explain concepts or theorize
- chase cast-iron repeatability the way a tutorial must (it may start
  mid-process, and assume a reasonable starting state)
- include background that does not serve the goal

**Test:** the title matches a sentence a real user would type into search.

---

## 3. Reference — information-oriented

**Analogy:** an encyclopedia entry on ginger. Facts about provenance, behaviour,
and properties. It does not teach you to cook with it.

**Purpose:** describe the machinery accurately, so a working user can look up a
fact and get back to work.

MUST:
- **mirror the structure of the codebase**, so the reader can navigate code and
  docs in parallel — this also exposes what is missing or stale
- be austere and consistent in structure, tone, and format across every entry
- state constraints, gotchas, and interactions
- describe classes, functions, parameters, return values, errors, config keys
- include the minimum usage needed to operate the thing (how to instantiate,
  how to invoke)
- stay accurate and current; wrong reference is worse than absent reference

MUST NOT:
- explain concepts
- teach how to accomplish a task
- contain opinion, speculation, or discussion

**Test:** every public surface appears, in the same shape, with no argument.
Generate it from source where possible — hand-maintained reference rots.

---

## 4. Explanation — understanding-oriented

**Analogy:** a book on food and cooking in the context of history, science, and
technology. It analyses; it considers multiple perspectives.

**Purpose:** illuminate the topic. Read at leisure, away from the keyboard.
Broadens the reader's understanding of *why*.

MUST:
- give context and background
- state design decisions and the reasons behind them
- cover technical and historical constraints ("we did it this way because in
  2019 the upstream API had no batch endpoint")
- weigh alternatives that were considered and rejected, and the trade-offs
- admit opinion, and attribute it

MUST NOT:
- instruct on performing a task
- act as reference material
- duplicate what the other three quadrants already do

**Scope:** unlike the other three, its boundaries are arbitrary — a topic is
whatever you judge a reasonable area to cover at once.

**Test:** it answers "why is it like this?" for someone who already knows how to
use it.

---

## Where each quadrant lives in a repo

| Quadrant     | Home                                                        |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Introduction | `README.md` — what this is, why the reader should care, which pain it removes, then links to the four sections. Keep it a doorway, not a manual. |
| Tutorial     | `docs/tutorials/` — usually just one, "getting started"      |
| How-to       | `docs/how-to/<how-to-x>.md` — grows over time, one per real question |
| Reference    | `docs/reference/` mirroring source layout, or generated from docstrings/types |
| Explanation  | `docs/explanation/`, architecture decision records (`docs/adr/`), `WHY.md` |

Extras that carry real weight:

- **`WHY.md`** (batman's ritual) is pure explanation quadrant: why this project
  should exist at all. Write it before the code, not after.
- **ADRs** are explanation, one decision per file, dated, including the rejected
  options. An ADR is the cheapest possible defence against re-litigating a
  settled decision six months later.
- **Code comments explain WHY, not WHAT.** The what is in the code; if the code
  is unclear, fix the code. The why cannot be recovered from the source — a
  comment naming the constraint, the bug it works around, or the reason the
  obvious approach fails is the highest-value comment there is.
- **`ponytail:` comments** name a deliberate shortcut and its upgrade path.
  Harvest them with `/ponytail-debt` rather than letting them rot.

## Practical rules

1. **Pick the quadrant before writing a line.** State it in the doc's frontmatter
   or heading if it helps.
2. **Update reference in the same commit as the code change.** Reference that
   lags the code is a liability.
3. **Do not write a tutorial for an unstable API.** It will break and burn trust.
4. **A missing how-to is a support question you will answer repeatedly.** Every
   second time you explain something in chat, it becomes a how-to.
5. **Docs are shared state.** Anything learned that the repo does not record goes
   into the repo — its `CLAUDE.md`, an ADR, or the relevant quadrant.

shared/clippings/evergreen-notes-turn-id.content:
Using evergreen notes in Obsidian has been the most impactful change to how I think.
Evergreen notes allow you to think about complex ideas by building them up from smaller composable ideas.
My evergreen notes have titles that distill each idea in a succinct and memorable way, that I can use in a sentence. For example:

A company is a superorganism
All input is error
Calmness is a superpower
Cross the chasm
Everything is a remix
Writing is telepathy
You have no obligation to your former self
etc

You don’t need to agree with the idea for it to become an evergreen note. Evergreen notes can be very short.
I have an evergreen note called Creativity is combinatory uniqueness that is built on top of another evergreen note:

If you believe Everything is a remix, then creativity is defined by the uniqueness and appeal of the combination of elements.

Evergreen notes turn ideas into objects. By turning ideas into objects you can manipulate them, combine them, stack them. You don’t need to hold them all in your head at the same time.

AI Coding Skill Reference
---
name: writing-code
description: Use for any code work — writing, adding, refactoring, fixing, reviewing, or documenting code. Routes to the right process skill for each phase, sets the documentation standard, defines when a change is actually done, and governs subagent and context spending.
when_to_use: implement, add a feature, fix a bug, refactor, write tests, build, debug, review a diff, write docs or a README, set up a new project, "why is this failing", "make it work"
---
 
# Code work
 
Read `references/documentation.md` before writing any documentation, README, or
docstring. Do not write docs from memory — the four-quadrant rules are specific.
 
## The loop
 
Per feature, in order. Each phase has a skill that owns it — use it, don't
improvise the phase from memory.
 
| Phase | Owner | Skip when |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Should this exist? | `batman-new` (new project/feature) | Bug fix, or scope already settled |
| 2. Understand the ask | `brainstorming`, or `requirements-clarity` if requirements are the fuzzy part | Intent is unambiguous and small |
| 3. Read the real flow | `Explore` subagent (wide search) or codegraph tools | Already have the context |
| 4. Plan | `writing-plans`; plan mode for anything multi-file | Single obvious edit |
| 5. Pick the smallest rung | `ponytail` ladder — always active | Never |
| 6. Test-first | `test-driven-development` | Trivial one-liner, or `ponytail`'s single runnable check is enough |
| 7. Implement one slice | — | Never: one slice at a time, each ending verifiable |
| 8. Verify with evidence | `verification-before-completion` | Never |
| 9. Document | `references/documentation.md` | Nothing user-facing or non-obvious changed |
| 10. Commit | `commit-work` / `caveman-commit` | Never; small commits, don't push unless asked |
 
Debugging enters at `systematic-debugging`, not at phase 1.
 
**Fix root causes.** A report names a symptom. Before editing, find every caller
of the function you're about to touch; one guard in the shared function beats a
guard in each caller and leaves no sibling still broken.
 
## Ask, or default
 
These pull in opposite directions, so the tiebreak is explicit:
 
- **Different readings produce materially different work** → ask, before writing.
  Architecture, data model, scope boundaries, anything hard to reverse.
- **A sensible default exists** → take it, name it in one line, keep going. Never
  stall on a choice you can default and flag.
- **Uncertain about a fact** → verify it with a command, a doc, or a search.
  Never silently assume, never hand the lookup back to the user.
 
Batch the questions. Ask at the point the answer is needed, not up front, and do
everything that doesn't depend on the answer first.
 
## Subagents
 
A subagent starts cold and re-derives context — it is the expensive path, not the
cheap one. Spawn one only when **the reading is large and the answer is small**.
 
- Good: "find every place we build the auth header" (`Explore`), sweeping an
  unfamiliar tree, a long research read.
- Bad: work you already have the context for, anything needing conversation
  history, or a task whose output is as large as its input.
- Delegate with a **specific question and a stated output shape**, not a topic.
  A vague prompt returns a vague summary and the reading has to be redone.
- Read-only fan-out → `Explore`. Design → `Plan`. Both skip CLAUDE.md to stay
  small, so restate any constraint they must respect in the prompt itself.
- Never delegate the final verification. Confirm that yourself.
 
Three custom agents exist for the recurring cases, each with a fixed output
shape so the answer comes back small:
 
| Agent | Use for | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `code-explorer` | locating symbols and callers in an unfamiliar tree | a `path:line` table, haiku, read-only |
| `code-reviewer` | a diff that's written but not yet trusted | `path:line — defect → fix`, preloads this skill, cannot edit |
| `test-runner` | running the suite, lint, or typecheck | `PASS`/`FAIL (n)` plus verbatim failures only |
 
Prefer these over `Explore` for code work — they load CLAUDE.md and
`rules/code.md`, so the constraints don't need restating.
 
## Definition of done
 
Not done until all of these are true:
 
1. The stated ask is complete — not the easy part of it. Anything left out is
   named explicitly, with the reason.
2. Tests written and **run**, with output seen. "Should pass" is not passing.
3. Lint and typecheck clean.
4. Non-trivial logic leaves one runnable check behind — an `assert`-based
   `demo()`/`__main__`, or one small `test_*.py`.
5. Docs updated in the same change, in the right quadrant.
6. Diff read start to finish. No unrelated edits, no drive-by reformatting.
7. Claims match reality: if tests fail, say so with the output; if a step was
   skipped, say that.
 
Never report success from expectation. Evidence before assertion.
 
## Context
 
Quality degrades past ~100k. Treat context as the scarce resource it is.
 
- One session per feature. `/compact` between chunks, fresh session on a pivot.
- Read the part of the file you need, not the whole file.
- Prefer the `LSP` tool and codegraph over grep-and-guess — real symbol data,
  fewer wrong turns, less reading. `code-explorer` for wide location sweeps.
- If `.codegraph/` exists in the project, read `~/.claude/codegraph.md` for the
  tool table and use those lookups instead of scanning files.
 
## Reach for the real tool
 
Do not describe, approximate, or reimplement a capability that already exists:
 
- **Library or framework specifics, any version question** → Context7. Even when
  the answer feels known; training data lags.
- **UI actually works?** → Playwright. Drive it like a user; read the console.
  Don't eyeball the code and declare it working.
- **Facts, current events, unfamiliar tooling** → Perplexity (`perplexity_search`
  for URLs/facts, `perplexity_research` for depth).
- **Over-engineering suspected** → `/ponytail-review` on the diff,
  `/ponytail-audit` on the repo.
- **Diff written but not yet trusted** → `code-reviewer`. Tests, lint, typecheck
  → `test-runner`. Neither can edit, so the report comes back honest.
- **Security is designed in, not bolted on.** For each feature answer: who may do
  this, what inputs exist, what can be abused, what data is sensitive. Then still
  do the final pass on critical flows.
 
## Security floor
 
Never simplify away: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents
data loss, authz checks, secrets hygiene (never in prompts, never in the repo),
accessibility basics. `ponytail` shortens solutions, never these.

shared/story-of-ai.title: Story of AI
shared/story-of-ai.content:
What is the story of AI, where are we going?
It’s a question that was uncomfortable to me for a long time. Because, simply, I had no idea!
I probably still don’t, but I can give it a shot.
I stumbled upon AI-2027, an AI prediction by experts made in 2025. I loved reading it, because it told a well made, coherent story. But naturally AI has evolved differently.
Notably I’d say it’s going faster.
If you don’t want to get a bit spoiled, go read it first, ai-2027.com/.
We already have deceptive AI, not in intent, but in capability. And we are at the stage where AI has become strong enough to easily hack software with our current world (unless I underestimate the cyber budget, which I doubt) - I see it code without making mistakes besides security ones, ironically.
There is talk of the necessity of dialogue between China and the USA, like with the nuclear threat.
This may be cause for despair. But as a friend told me, we have the technology necessary to resolve the world’s issues if we focused them properly.
It’s easier than ever to write software
I just feel like capitalism is outdated.
Linkedin post on this:
Stop making AI better. Make it better.
When I was at the TRAIL gala when they asked: what do we really want to use AI for? It made me think.
Geertrui Mieke De Ketelaere said that experts should make the invisible visible. So let me try.
AI is a tool. Right now, it can automate workflows, connect to everything you own, deal with astronomical amounts of information, and take action on it. It can code, plan, critique, research, even hack, and all of that exceptionally well. Also, unlike code, anyone can query it in their own language.
That’s good enough for me. I mean this. Who needs it to be so good that it fully replaces us? I like being at the helm of my job, and I like my job. I must agree with Louis de Diesbach, I don’t want AGI.
We’re seeing AI described as “rogue” lately. But it’s not rogue. It just has new capabilities - like being better at deceiving, better at persuading - and it uses them. That’s not a bug, that’s what happens when you keep pushing for more powerful without pushing for more responsible. It’s powerful enough.
So what do I mean by “make it better”? Make it more energy efficient. More compressed. Better guardrails.
Take our time to learn the wise ways to use it (not only the optimal ways), and share them. Not rush to add it everywhere just because we can.
Here is one of the pre-prompts I give Claude: “take a deep breath, and do this step by step.” We could all use that advice.
You’re allowed to have an opinion on this. In fact, please do.
As for me, I don’t want to optimize the human out of the equation.

shared/tv/hackers-(1995).title: Hackers (1995)
shared/tv/hackers-(1995).content:
Great movie, shows you what being a hacker is all about, with heart and the will and power to change the world for good, together, with that really nice hacker vibe.
The visual style of the movie is pretty good, too!
Taken from my linkedin post, a modern take on this movie:

First of all I’ll say it’s a banger and you should watch it if you haven’t yet. I won’t spoil anything.
The heroes of this movie are kids, and it’s inspired by real hacks. It reminded me of my university cyber courses. About a time when cybersecurity laws and rules were immature or inexistant.
When the new generation - those who adapt tje fastest - was born in the age of the internet and thought to use the systems differently than intended, it worked. They got in, because the systems were designed in a naive way. Thankfully the kids mostly weren’t malicious, and the world did not depend on the web as it does today. Still, they crashed the early internet with the Morris worm.
The same thing happened again already; a teenager hacked into 6 million accounts. In cyber we learn that the least protected is what hackers will target. For a while that was fishing attacks, now exploitation is becoming much easier and more common.
So what can we learn from what we did back then? We came up with measures, laws, trainings, designed systems differently, used encryption, and tried our security ourselves. Banks are very much ahead in this, but what about most companies?
Please, don’t be alarmed. Be aware. The time has come to invest into security again. This time, it’s all about AI. Funnily enough, I’m using the same techniques attackers are reported doing: using AI to speed up breaking into systems (except I take the money upfront, with consent, and much less).
The issue is that companies often only worry about security when it’s too late and they’ve been breached already. There is the technical debt, but there is also the security debt, and hackers will be sure to come collect it one day!
Everything is faster and cheaper with AI. We should use this power to make better products than ever. Those who do are and will be those who come out on top.

shared/thoughts/catalyst.title: Catalyst
shared/thoughts/catalyst.content:
Hello stranger.
It’s a wild world. Did you have time to catch up?
I’m also overwhelmed at times.
Here are the most impactful words, videos, speeches, peoples I’ve ever come across.
First, let’s read this recent report. This is how AI can be used.
Perplexity
Former Palantir workers condemn company’s work with Trump administration
“Coordinated space and cyber operations effectively disrupted communications and sensor networks across the area of responsibility, leaving the adversary without the ability to see, coordinate, or respond”
That’s how powerful AI is.
But don’t despair. Let’s try to see it differently. After a bit more information. It’ll be more positive right after I promise.

This technology, this tool, is powerful, yes - so is whatever device you’re reading this from. And everything behind it to make it work.
It’s all a matter of what you use it for.
To unite, or to divide? It’s the only question.
Reminds me of this beautiful video that gives a new way of seeing the world:

And here is my favorite speech of all time:

The speech still is relevant today. It’s time to go to the moon again. Not because we have to, but because we can.
I don’t believe in existential crises anymore. I believe it’s just an itch to do something.
I’m a hacker, I can understand and use this tool. I can teach you, so you have autonomy in today’s world. But that’s not all.
The only thing we need… is to talk about it.
Humanity’s will has been eroded by time. We forgot to dream.
What do you want the moon to be?
Maybe we can’t reach it. But let’s not wait for others to do something. What kind of world do you want?
We’re not all going to have the same answer for that, but I’m sure we all want to prosper and be happy? Are we, now? Then let’s do something and stop despairing about it.

Yes you can do it. If you ever doubt in your humanity, read this:
www.britannica.com/biography/Helen-Keller
What should you do? Well you don’t have to do anything, yet you get to do everything, here’s a video on that:

You already know what to do
Take good care of yourself.
Take good care of others.
Do what brings meaning.
Join or make communities.
Learn what you don’t know… We have free access to an oracle that is connected to all of human knowledge… Use it wisely.
And use the wisdom of the past.
Don’t fear death. Fear a worthless life
Let us learn from the stoics a bit more in fact

But don’t disconnect from yourself either. I love Allan Watts for that:

You’re probably not going to see what I mean yet.
That’s alright.
Let it be a seed.
We’re all on this boat together.
What inspired you in your life? I’d love to know.
What do you think about digital minimalism?

shared/thoughts/education/critique-of-th.title: Critique of the system
shared/thoughts/education/critique-of-th.content:
Before proposing a new system I’ll point out what’s wrong with the current one, which hasn’t changed much, despite the world evolving around it.
Firstly, for most education I know, a lot of importance is put on remembering - but we’re not taught how to do it well.
Secondly, some subjects like maths or sciences are covered, but so long as students have to question the point of it they’re not ready to learn as much.
Thirdly, there’s a focus on being able to have answers in the exams and whatnot, by oneself, and not to question things and cooperate with others. Instead, a lot of time is often spent sitting, at home or at school.
Finally, there are a lot of things that are expected to be taught by the parents, but who knows what they’re teaching!
In this context it’s hard to keep the student’s attention and make them want to learn and participate in today’s society, especially if you contrast this outdated system with social phones’ addictiveness.
If we look at the Montessori model by contrast, it has more freedom for young children, letting them choose more and helping them become fully autonomous individuals. The issue is it’s intended for kindergarden but there are things to be taught later on, too.

shared/thoughts/education/index.title: Education
shared/thoughts/education/index.content:
Why Education Matters
Education shapes who we are—it’s what sets humans apart in complexity. Yet, it varies across countries, schools, and families, leaving us unsure of the best approach. Many books trace adult struggles back to childhood, showing that early experiences can take a lifetime to heal. Works like The Biology of Transcendence, Emotional Intelligence, A More Beautiful Question, Moonwalking with Einstein and Montessori principles offer insights into how we learn and grow
Critique of the system
What should every school teach to prepare children for adult life? Instead of rigid structures, imagine themes spread intelligently—flexible classes that kids can enter anytime or even organize themselves.
Of course, open-ended learning has its risks. But the more we box people in, the less adaptable they become. Giving up control can be daunting—when was the last time it truly happened? The 1960s?
Forcing kids into rigid systems their entire lives doesn’t guarantee responsible adults. Authority figures demanding respect only teach obedience; what happens when they’re no longer there? True responsibility comes from understanding, not compulsion.
With that in mind, here are the proposed themes of a new education system:
Themes
shared/thoughts/education/index.description: Why Education Matters Education shapes who we are—it’s what sets humans apart in complexity.

shared/thoughts/education/themes.title: Themes
shared/thoughts/education/themes.content:
A Holistic and Integrated Education System
Education should nurture creativity, curiosity, emotional intelligence, and real-world skills while allowing children to remain true to their inner selves. This system is built on interconnected themes that provide a comprehensive learning experience.
1. Artistic Expression
A course designed for maximum freedom, allowing children to explore and express themselves beyond words. Through music, drawing, outdoor activities, and other creative outlets, students learn to channel their imagination and emotions. Adults, in turn, can learn from their innocence and dreams.
2. Language and Literature
Reading and writing are essential skills, but they should be taught through books and materials that inspire and engage children. Literature should be a window into diverse worlds, fueling imagination, critical thinking, and the ability to understand one another.
A book like the art of conversation can help us have better talks with others and ourselves.
3. Cultural Awareness
A well-rounded education should not be confined to a single cultural perspective. Students should explore histories, traditions, and ways of life from around the world. A comparative approach to past and present cultures fosters global awareness and empathy.
4. Emotional Awareness and Communication
Teaching children to understand their emotions, express their needs, and seek support is fundamental. Instead of suppressing feelings or taking them out on others, they should learn healthy communication, conflict resolution, and self-reflection. Meditation and mindfulness can be used to feel ourselves and others more.
5. Real-World Skills and Responsibilities
An education system should prepare students for adulthood by integrating real-life skills into daily learning.

Politics: A democratic school system where students can engage in decision-making and governance.
Responsibility: Participation in maintaining shared spaces fosters accountability.
Philosophy & Self-Trust: Encouraging independent thought and self-reflection.
Health & Well-being: Lessons on nutrition, relationships, and overcoming challenges like addiction.

6. Curiosity and Science
Science should be a gateway to curiosity and exploration, not just a subject. This course encourages questioning, critical thinking, and hands-on discovery. Learning should extend beyond scientific concepts to encompass all disciplines that fuel curiosity about the world.
This will also include techniques such as the mind map, memory palace etc to understand and remember all information.
7. Physical Activity and Sports
Students should have the freedom to choose between team sports that teach collaboration and solo sports that build discipline. Movement is essential for physical and mental health, and sports can be integrated into other areas of learning.
8. Relaxation and Leisure
Learning is important, but so is being a child. Relaxation activities—whether watching movies, engaging in casual conversation, or meditating—make school enjoyable and fulfilling. These moments also provide indirect learning opportunities while ensuring students remain engaged.
shared/thoughts/education/themes.description: A Holistic and Integrated Education System Education should nurture creativity, curiosity, emotional intelligence, and real-world skills while allowing children to remain true to their inner selves.

shared/thoughts/happiness.title: Happiness
shared/thoughts/happiness.content:
Enlightenment cannot be grasped and kept. It cannot be the goal of the journey, only its light.
Just like happiness on the horizon keeps moving away as we head towards it.
All is already here, but, distracted by the fog of life, we fail to see it.
No human before us had more things. Or potential. To live long, to travel… I realize I am lucky in those things, and try to give back.
Happy is not in things. They barely satisfy us, until we crave for more.
Even friends or love can’t just give it to us. They give us the strength to find it in ourselves. Even after finding it, we must keep the beacon lit.
Only through hardship could I find strength.
For me, enlightenment is not a choice as much as it is a necessity. My body fights itself. This fatigue cannot be beaten by rest alone. Yet I cannot always push my limits.
Alexandre Darius The Great
A great protector of the people, but also my own enemy. So fitting.
I share because I am not scared. Because for too long I thought this was my struggle alone, but we have so much in common. Because I healed enough to help others. Because for 12 years, since WOW told it to me, I had to tell myself “guardez la tête haute” until now I finally do it, whole.
I never once lost the incarnate will to live. After focusing inwards for so long, I can focus outwards.
We are one, but if we are not then… Nemo Me Impune Lacessit
Formlessness is freedom
Acceptation is peace
Vulnerability is strength
Uniqueness is purpose

shared/thoughts/relationships/non-violen.title: Non violent communication
shared/thoughts/relationships/non-violen.content:
Barely 1/3rd through this book and it’s already better than anything I’ve read!
I feel like this should be taught at schools.
I used to be wary of this kind of method.
Now I’m ready for it. It helps in understanding how to communicate better, something we may all feel like we do a good enough job at already. I didn’t.
It is more than a process, it is a lifestyle of avoiding judgment, expressing ourselves clearly and understanding others’ feelings and needs.
That being said, the process itself is roughly what follows:

Make observations, without judgment, without evaluation. If we mix observations with judgment, the other person might feel the need to be defensive.
Here is a made up example:
Instead of saying “you don’t care about me”, we can try to say what inspired that thought. For example: “You don’t cook for me”
Share our feelings on that. The impact which said observation, that could be a behavior someone has, an action someone did, has on us. It’s important to find out what the feeling really is with the right word.
Continuing the example from before,
Instead of inferring how the other is thinking or feeling, say “I don’t really feel appreciated”
Express needs. It can be hard to figure them out truly, and to express vulnerability by saying them out loud. Others should react with empathy.
“I need attention, love in this form or another”
Make a request. Try to respect other’s needs as well, naturally. Also phrase it in a positive way, asking for what we want and not focusing on what we don’t want. It would ideally be a concrete and precise request.
“I would like you to cook for me once a week”

To me it feels like the issue that often comes into play is that we tend to make shortcuts, simplifying things, and expecting others to be able to unwrap our thoughts, to know our needs.
In the case where only one person uses this method, they can try to find the feelings and needs from what is said, leading to the person feeling heard, at which point true discussion can begin.
And we can do it with ourselves, too!
Looking at the needs and feelings that made us behave a certain way, instead of judgments and “should have done X”

shared/thoughts/relationships/on-attract.title: On attraction
shared/thoughts/relationships/on-attract.content:
For clarty’s sake, I separated this from the main topic of relationships, for a short mention.
Why are we attracted to someone?
There’s 4 elements I can see, after learning about it for a year:

What we admire (things we want to do and they can do)
Compatibility (values, somehow they’re written on their face, how we interact)
The bond with the person (what we live together, how they make us feel)
Their value as a mate (status, beauty, confidence, age - not the same for men or women)

And of course are they like our parents? Secure attachment styles are better but that may not be our own.
We may consider it normal to go with someone we are attracted to initially, as seems to be the societal norm nowadays. It has not always been the case. And of course we can choose who we want to date, it’s not just a matter of attraction.

shared/thoughts/relationships/index.title: Relationships
shared/thoughts/relationships/index.content:
Going beyond attraction, what makes a relationship work or not? What makes it a good one?
On attraction
Context:
Attraction can be easy to build. But what happens after that? At some point, we have to ask ourselves: What do we really want in a relationship? What makes it meaningful?
It used to be that there were rules in society, like marriage, establishing what we can or cannot do. I won’t give an opinion on them, but there was some sort of order. And now it feels like that’s been taken away, and everyone is lost. In that context, many are losing, because of unspoken things not being agreed on, because of having different definitions of love, of having different needs etc.
There seem to be so many expectations today around a romantic relationship, where a partner is sometimes expected to bring connection, want, be a good friend, what a whole village had to before, sometimes even things that we should perhaps be bringing to ourselves.
I’m going to be asking questions and presenting my perspective on it, in the hopes of helping others shape their own.
Let the questioning begin! Casual or serious dating?
If we engage in casual relationships, it’s important to make sure both people truly are on the same page. Are we being honest with ourselves and each other about what we want?
If intimacy becomes so easy, doesn’t it make it less special?
Perhaps it is good to have some fun in our youth, to try things without taking them so seriously. I personally won’t. However it is true that it takes trying to see if a relationship can work, once we find the right person.
That said to me it feels like many are disoriented by today’s dating world, unsure what they want and what to expect of others, perhaps just trying to do like others, or giving up on dating entirely.
So what can make a relationship endure?
Attraction isn’t permanent, it fluctuates. So if attraction is the only thing holding a relationship together, it won’t last. After some time, the ‘halo effect’ of attraction will fade, and we will see the real person beyond our idealized version of them, after 4 months or so. That’s when we face a choice: do we accept them as they are?
If we want it to work, having a common project, a common goal or at least interest in the other’s goal can help ensure staying together in the long term, when life pulls us apart or disputes happen, as they will.
Most important of all, we must know what our partner has to say about this question: what is love?
Love involves growth. We naturally influence each other, shaping how we see the world, who we are, what we do and how we connect. But the key is to grow together while still staying true to ourselves. So a good question would be do you like what you would shape yourself into, with that person?
It’s also better to not be held down by past relationships for that reason, otherwise we can’t really let ourselves go, we’re not truly ready for a new experience, and other people deserve someone who is ready. If we don’t work enough on ourselves, or don’t have the right person, we may not dare to open up, to change, to be vulnerable, to grow.
By the same logic, it is important to be connected to ourselves. It is hard to truly empathize with others when we lack the mental space and peace of mind to do so.
I’m not saying this to make anyone feel guilty but I think we should be willing to give to others what we expect from them.
What to take from this?
What I’m saying is self knowledge is key for our relationship with ourselves. For this I found that meditation can help, to find ourselves in the silence, to live with ourselves, know who we are, what we want. I think it’s also important to have enough self-respect to not pursue those that are unavailable, to have the strength to face our potentially problematic attachment styles. To know what we want from a relationship. Most of that we figure out by giving ourselves space to think and not rush from one relationship to the other - the deepest the love the longer it will take to move on. We can journal to go further in our self knowledge.
For our relationship with others, communication is key. To share our needs, to be understood. The book non violent communication can help for that, with time and patience. Understand each other can be a challenge, and a mood where we can say how we feel without too much fear of being judged can really help.
Non violent communication
Oh and it’s probably a good idea to make sure both have enough time to grow, listen, empathize and spend time together.
“Love is what you offer another person when you’re already happy.” Alan Waltz
Behind the feeling of I, beyond need.
I’d like to point out that relationships do not only exist in a romantic context. We have some sort of relationship with every friend, with our family etc. They will have unspoken or spoken agreements, and communication is important there, too, for boundaries and the benefit of everyone. Of course there’s no need to worry about it all the time, but saying when something is wrong and being open minded is where it’s at!
Do feel free to send this whole text to AI to ask it to add examples or explain in more details.
(Or just ask me directly old school haha)
www.youtube.com/watch
For those who want to wait for the perfect person.
And remember, Amor Vincit Omnia sed Cura Te Ipsum
For the rational ones
m.youtube.com/watch#

shared/thoughts/video-games.title: Video games
shared/thoughts/video-games.content:
I went to a debate about video games, entertainment and their role in our culture, with 4 different experts, on the effect on adults and children, and with movie clips to spark discussion. This is what it inspired me to write, maybe it can inspire you too!
Video games… are they really a part of our culture, or just some form of entertainment? How do they compare to movies, music, books and stories? What is entertainment even for?
Let me take you in a journey that goes all the way back to antic Greece, and the notions of catharsis and memesis.
open.spotify.com/track/5TXuCg39hYvbTiEF1juyEY%0A

On playing

It’s quite critical for children to play.
One example of this from a very young age would be “pickaboo”, the game where we create a bit of tension (where is mama?) and then resolve it (here!) creating laughter.
Games are to learn to live, not in a theoretical way but in a fun, diverse and evolving one.
Adolescents will also play, hopefully discovering their identity, trying team sports etc as they do so. With art, even?
That’s where video games can truly shine, as a portal to another life! Suddenly we’re no longer just Max, the 10 years old, instead we become a God, an adventurer and more! Even those who don’t have the most fruitful of imaginations can have just as much fun.
The potential is great, for instance here is a text-based “game” to discover ourselves.


Memesis, and the interest of fear

Let’s go back to when we were kids. Who didn’t like stories?
Surely stories are good for the imagination, but I won’t dive into that here. The way they connect with video games is that they can also teach us to deal with fear, by being confronted with a weaker version of it, a simple reflection. That way when something really scary comes, we’ll be more ready.

Stories can put us in someone else’ shoes. They can also let us explore another identity, which can be freeing, explorative, especially at a young age when we’re looking for ours.
In that context video games are the medium where we will be the most immersed into a different situation. The most distracted from this life, in another one. But is that really a good thing?

Immersion

In games we’re fully present. Time is altered, there is no dullness, no boring parts, time is accelerated.
We get to fully feel in someone else’s place in a way that’s stronger than what movies can do. We get to actually make choices, act.
Naturally, it can be an escape from life, as it will allow us not to no longer be ourselves, but at least to focus on other things, to forget our problems. But also to be intellectually, visually stimulated.

There is something that must be addressed, however. Not all games are the same. Some try to trap us in a dark loop, and should be avoided. Heck, it’s not only games, social media can do it too.
Much like social media, games can allow us to make friends, especially for those of a more introverted nature, offering a most welcomed slight distance from others, like it is all happening in a world of its own.
However it is good to note that both are quite recent, and as it often is the case, when a new addition is made to human culture, some take a distance from it, and rightfully so. We can see this with AI, we fear the impact it might have on society. So much so we did some movies about it like terminator. But why do we create them?

Catharsis, and why we create and consume

It’s quite simple: we create culture to express what we want to communicate to others, to have an influence on the collective culture of what others think, and we consume them for the opposite, to feel those things others want us to feel, to expand our perspective. For instance, after a time of war, many will turn to writing to process what happened to them, to share, and hopefully be understood, to impact culture.
When we consume it, it has the potential to shape our world view, and it can come in many forms, just like we can feel and express in many forms, beyond just words.
There are great movies like Soul and Shawshank redemption, great games like endless sky and baldur’s gate, great musics like classical music… great art like Van Gogh and …
Which ones we like can say a lot about us.

Isn’t life a video game of sorts? No other games can compare with its depth, with its beauty, its storytelling and countless possibilities. Shouldn’t we be playful with it, try things, spice up conversation?
And at other times, shouldn’t we sometimes try to sit with the silence, instead of rushing to divert ourselves? It’s a long game!
Of course, life is more than just a game. A theater play, perhaps? If so, what character do you play? What does your story tell?

shared/thoughts/yesterday's-world.title: Yesterday's world
shared/thoughts/yesterday's-world.content:
Like it or not, AI is here. Yet some places, like schools Education are still living in the world of the past. For schools, it feels like they’re still in the industrial era, training us for repetitive work with a bit updated manuals, but the same structure still.
Yet we live in an era beyond these things. It’s easier than it’s ever been to learn something new, re-orient, and whilst that may cause more issues deciding what to do, it also means that hard skills are not as required anymore, if at all, for tasks, the kind of people who performs the task matters more.
Going further, interviews ask about your experience but in this amazing world you can literally check out 10 projects you could do right now that would advance you readily.
You do, however, need to choose what it is you’re doing. You need to pick a decision.
Ikigai The Japanese Art of Happiness is the closest thing to help reflect on that, but I think in practice it needs to be done with a pen and paper; with a friend and a drink; with an older person and their experience; between yourself and your dreams.
I like smelling what people really care about. The stuff they can talk about all day.. Please talk to me about it, show me that passion. Noticing how little you know about yourself can be daunting, but if you travel through that Forest of knowledge you’ll arrive on the other side wiser and more confident than ever.

travel/artists.title: Artists
travel/artists.content:
16 artists from all over the world coming here in Ladakh, seeing it from an external perspective. Speaking and thinking with their hands for all of us.

Artists speak and materialize what the people feel.
They talked about fear of technology and how it cannot replace emotions and human connection. How they went through the difficulty here in Ladakh too.
They shared with each other and spoke in turn.
If you ask, why do this? I will say, why do anything?
Because we are humans, and let’s not forget that and lose our connection.
White scarves are given to guests of honor as a mark of respect.

I talked with the french person who sang as we all hummed together, he recommended trying out the underground place that shows acrobatic arts in a static way for us to experiment.
I was confused but it was interesting.

Another conversation, technology is coming to Ladakh, and they want it, so who are we as outsiders to say they shouldn’t get it?
Yet behind it there may be some bad things. It’s just a tool, of course… Like a knife.
And the culture of the world… I see it unifying… I see people becoming passive because of their mindless consumptions that stops them from being themselves… They no longer spend times on making culture much…
Whatever happens my friend,
Never let the light in your eyes
Become a hollow…

travel/back-to-the-nest.title: Back to the nest
travel/back-to-the-nest.content:
Back to the nest!
Worries are behind
This is a bit of a special post
I want to share this inspiring poetry that found me, and another one, with connected pictures
Feel free to scroll past if that’s not your thing
(I made the second image with AI)
Second sight, by David Whyte
“Sometimes, you need the ocean light,
and colours you’ve never seen before
painted through an evening sky.
Sometimes you need your God
to be a simple invitation
not a telling word of wisdom.
Sometimes you need only the first shyness
that comes from being shown things
far beyond your understanding,
so that you can fly and become free
by being still and by being still here.
And then there are times you want to be
brought to ground by touch
and touch alone.
To know those arms around you
and to make your home in the world
just by being wanted.
To see eyes looking back at you,
as eyes should see you at last,
seeing you, as you always wanted to be seen,
seeing you, as you yourself
had always wanted to see the world.”
And here’s part of another one, more down to earth:
Genius of the crowd by Charles Bukowski
“beware the preachers
beware the knowers
beware those who are always reading books
beware those who either detest poverty
or are proud of it
beware those quick to praise
for they need praise in return
beware those who are quick to censor
they are afraid of what they do not know
beware those who seek constant crowds for
they are nothing alone
beware the average man the average woman
beware their love, their love is average
seeks average
but there is genius in their hatred
there is enough genius in their hatred to kill you
to kill anybody
not wanting solitude
not understanding solitude
they will attempt to destroy anything
that differs from their own
not being able to create art
they will not understand art
they will consider their failure as creators
only as a failure of the world
not being able to love fully
they will believe your love incomplete
and then they will hate you
and their hatred will be perfect
like a shining diamond
like a knife
like a mountain
like a tiger
like hemlock
their finest art”
Make of it what you will
These are the two poetry that just found me

travel/burning-man/index.title: Burning man
travel/burning-man/index.content:
It all starts with a dream.
In it, I enter a prison.
There’s a few people here, but I don’t pay much attention to them. Instead, I go to a white room, and discuss with an inmate there.
“I’m trapped in here,” he says, “because I can’t control my pulsions.”
Then I wake up, but the dream continues…
I. Soft Wake Up
II. 5 hours in Paris
III. The Dharma Bum
VI. A “virgin” has arrived
V. What I Learned from the Burners

Together we all brought the place back to its original state, and then it was time for farewell hugs.
I came back in a car, as I was hoping, planned last minute. As I’m writing this, it feels like some important chapter of my life just ended.
“The search.”
I’m ready now. Whatever comes.
“What’s the name of this story of your future you told me?” Maria, the story doctor, asked me.
“The final climb.”
As I get back home, the pictures of my childhood are suddenly there, waiting for me, reflecting change within.
When I came back from Japan, I moved in a new house. It was a bit empty, but not anymore. How fitting.
